title: How your spell checker fixes a typo it's never seen
description:
A classic spell checker keeps no list of typos. Over 80% of misspellings are a single slip (a letter missing, an extra one, a wrong one, or two letters swapped), so for 'teh' it generates every word one slip away: 187 guesses for a 3-letter word (54n + 25). Only 8 of them are in its word list, and of those 'the' appears 79,809 times in a million words of books, 'ten' 219 times, so it picks 'the'. Peter Norvig's version of this fits in about half a page of code and fixed 68% of a 400-typo test set.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py) on Norvig's big.txt corpus. Sources: Peter Norvig, How to Write a Spelling Corrector (norvig.com/spell-correct.html); Damerau, Communications of the ACM (1964).

The math behind real problems, twice a day. Subscribe and the next one finds you.

Damerau 1964: 'more than 80% were a result of a single error of one of the four types' (insertion, deletion, substitution, transposition) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damerau%E2%80%93Levenshtein_distance, fetched 2026-11-28)

beats.say: Your spell checker never saw your typo. It fixes it anyway.
There's no list of every mistake. Instead, it makes every mistake you could have made. On purpose.
More than 80% of typos are one slip. A letter missing, an extra one, a wrong one, or two swapped.
Say you typed T, E, H.
beats.caption: Say you typed "teh".

beats.say: Undo every possible slip. Drop each letter. Swap each pair. Try all 26 letters in every spot.
That's 187 guesses. Almost all of them junk.
Throw out everything that isn't in its word list. Only 8 are left.
But ten and tea are one slip away too. So which did you mean?
Count them in a million words of books. The shows up 79,809 times. Ten, just 219.
